title: Oil Just Posted Its Steepest Quarterly Drop Since 2020 — and India May Be the Biggest Winner
excerpt: Brent crude has crashed 43% from its Iran war peak to $71 a barrel, erasing the entire geopolitical risk premium. For the world's third-largest oil importer, the implications for inflation, the rupee, and the fiscal balance are enormous.
body:
Brent crude fell below $72 a barrel on Wednesday, its lowest level in more than four months, as progress in U.S.-Iran talks in Doha eased supply concerns and pushed oil to its steepest quarterly decline since the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The benchmark has now given back virtually the entire war premium. At $71.35, Brent is trading almost exactly where it was on February 27 — the day before the U.S.-Israeli offensive against Iran began. From its April peak of $126.41, the collapse amounts to a 43% decline, one of the sharpest reversals in oil market history.

"The negotiations currently taking place in Qatar are perceived as being positive, and that has allowed prices to drift further," said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen. "There is a chance that we could see even lower prices."

## How the War Premium Evaporated

The arithmetic of the crash is straightforward. When Iranian military action closed the Strait of Hormuz in early March, roughly 20% of global oil supply was choked off overnight. Brent surged past $120, inventories drew down sharply, and analysts raised their forecasts five months running.

The turning point came on June 17, when the United States and Iran agreed to an interim memorandum: a 60-day ceasefire, a commitment to reopen the Strait, and a framework for broader negotiations. Since then, stranded tankers have begun moving, Gulf exports have resumed, and the market has rapidly repriced.

The process has not been smooth. As recently as last weekend, Iran struck a supertanker carrying Qatari oil, prompting U.S. retaliatory strikes on 10 Iranian military targets. But with both sides returning to the table in Doha — President Trump said Wednesday that meetings had gone well — the market is treating the ceasefire as durable enough to trade on.

Analysts have now begun cutting their 2026 oil price forecasts for the first time since the war began. Morgan Stanley models an implied global surplus of 4.8 million barrels per day by 2027. The International Energy Agency expects global supply to surge by 8 million barrels per day next year, dwarfing demand growth of just 2 million.

## India's Macro Windfall

No major economy benefits more from cheaper oil than India. The country imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, making its fiscal health, current account balance, and inflation trajectory all highly sensitive to the price of a barrel of Brent.

The numbers are already moving. HSBC now forecasts a $25 billion balance of payments surplus for the fiscal year ending March 2027 — a dramatic swing from two years of deficit. Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points, lowered its inflation projection by 20 basis points, and expects a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP.

India's 10-year government bond yield fell to 6.72% this week, on track for its steepest monthly decline in nearly seven years. Foreign investors have bought nearly $3 billion of Fully Accessible Route bonds in June alone — the highest monthly inflow on record — attracted by the improved macro backdrop and the government's decision to remove taxes on foreign bond investment.

"The all-in FX package to attract inflows and the fall in oil prices have flipped the BoP outlook," HSBC said in a note.

## The Rupee Recovery

The rupee has been a direct beneficiary. After hitting a record low near 97 per dollar in May — when oil was above $120 — the currency has recovered to around 94.50, posting its first quarterly gain since March 2025 and ranking among Asia's best-performing currencies in June.

The recovery reflects more than just oil. The Reserve Bank of India extended a subsidised forex swap facility for banks' overseas borrowings and allowed lenders to offer credit to non-residents against foreign-currency deposits. Combined with the crude windfall, these measures have stabilised sentiment.

"The combination of lower crude, rupee stability and measures to draw foreign inflows has improved sentiment and liquidity," said Ajit Banerjee, president and chief investment officer at Shriram Life Insurance.

## Russia's Growing Share

One notable shift: Indian refiners have been aggressively increasing purchases of Russian crude to offset Middle Eastern supply disruptions. Russian oil imports surged to a record 2.70 million barrels per day in June, accounting for more than half of India's total imports, up from 36.5% in May.

The strategic calculation is clear — discounted Russian barrels provide a buffer against supply uncertainty. But the concentration risk is real, and the geopolitics are delicate. India's balancing act between Western allies and Russian energy dependence remains one of the most watched diplomatic dynamics in global commodity markets.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

The oil crash has improved India's investment case on almost every dimension that had worried foreign funds. Average allocations to India among emerging market funds had dropped below 10% in April — the lowest since early 2021 — from a peak of 17.5% in August 2024. That tide is now turning, with U.S.-listed India-focused ETF inflows turning positive last week for the first time in over a month.

But risks remain. The U.S.-Iran ceasefire is fragile — "we need to see sustained earnings recovery coming through," cautioned Ninghui Liu of State Street. India's June rainfall deficit of 43% could still crimp rural demand and food inflation. And expectations of U.S. Federal Reserve rate hikes later in 2026 continue to pressure IT stocks, which fell 9.6% in June.

For NRI investors, the oil decline is unambiguously positive for Indian fixed income, banking stocks, and consumer sectors. The question is whether it proves durable enough to reverse the broader equity outflows that have defined the first half of 2026.

**Sources:** *Reuters; Barron's; Wall Street Journal; The Hindu Business Line; HSBC Research; Goldman Sachs*
